part_title: How Large Language Models Predict and Sample Tokens
review_basis: Original Module 04 numbered WebP slides 4–7 individually inspected: actual labels, diagrams and example probabilities narrated in visual sequence.

scenes.title: Large language models (LLMs)
scenes.narration: On this slide we separate how a large language model learns from how it answers. Look at the left training panel. A text corpus is a large collection of books, articles, websites and other writing. Tokenization splits text into smaller pieces called tokens. A token can be a word, part of a word, or punctuation; the example cloud storage may be split into multiple pieces. The neural network then adjusts learned numerical weights to capture language patterns. These weights are not a verified encyclopedia of facts. Move to the inference panel on the right. A person asks the trained model to summarize an article about cloud storage. The model predicts and generates a response one token at a time, based on the prompt and the tokens it has already produced. The bottom row names other tasks the same model may perform: summarization, translation and question answering. Training is the expensive learning phase; inference is using the trained model for a new request. A fluent summary may still omit key details or invent a fact, so compare important statements with the supplied article. Question: does the model learn entirely new general weights each time somebody asks for a summary? Typically no. That prompt is an inference request.

scenes.title: How a language model predicts tokens
scenes.narration: Read the top as a repeating five-step loop. The model receives the current context, estimates probabilities for possible next tokens, selects one token, appends it to the context, and repeats. Context is all the text considered for the next prediction within the model's available window. On the bottom left, the context says Amazon S3 is. The illustrative candidate table assigns a probability of zero point five zero to the token a and smaller probabilities to other candidate tokens. The selected example is a, so the context becomes Amazon S3 is a. On the bottom right, the model runs another prediction. This time the candidate service has probability zero point four zero and is selected, producing Amazon S3 is a service. The candidates changed because the context changed. Notice that a selection can involve sampling instead of always taking the top candidate, depending on generation settings. These probabilities are educational examples, not measurements from an actual production model. The loop helps explain why a model can write coherent text and why its wording may change between runs. Quick check: does a forty-percent next-token probability mean that the completed statement has forty-percent factual accuracy? No. Token likelihood and factual verification are different things.

scenes.title: Generative language models: choosing a word
scenes.narration: Now consider the input sentence at left: After the rain, the streets were, followed by a blank. In the middle the model assigns an illustrative probability to each possible next word or token. Wet has zero point four zero, flooded zero point two five, slippery zero point one five, empty zero point one zero and muddy zero point one zero. Together the displayed probabilities add to one. The diagram selects wet and appends it to the context on the right. This is an example of a next-token decision, not a rule that the highest candidate always wins. The right-hand notes explain three things. First, context affects probabilities: a different starting sentence would produce a different distribution. Second, sampling controls such as temperature, top k and top p influence which candidates are considered or favored. Third, a low-probability token is not impossible. A model might choose muddy even though wet is shown as more likely. At the bottom the important teaching point is that generation is conditional on context and selection settings. Decision question: is a token with probability zero point ten necessarily wrong? No; it is simply less likely under this illustrative distribution.

scenes.title: Sampling the next token: worked example
scenes.narration: This worked example shows the full autoregressive loop. That word means each output step is informed by previously generated tokens. Start at panel one on the left. The current context reads After the rain, the streets were flooded. The illustrative candidate distribution shows and at zero point four two, but at zero point one eight, punctuation at zero point one two and several lower-probability continuations. These values are invented for teaching and sum to one. In panel two, the sample selected for this run is and. Notice the note that different runs may select different tokens; generation is not necessarily deterministic. In panel three the new context now ends with flooded and. The model predicts again: the is zero point two eight, cars zero point two four, people zero point one eight and several other possibilities fill out the distribution. Follow the large curved arrow along the bottom back to the beginning: append, recompute, sample and continue until the sequence stops. Sampling can yield varied natural writing, but it does not establish whether the text is true. Check: if the context changes, should we expect the exact same next-token probability distribution? No, because the model conditions its prediction on the updated context.
